newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Aid group says it fears US stance on mines is ploy.
newsitem.headline: Aid group says it fears US stance on mines is ploy.

text.p: French-Belgian aid organisation Handicap International on Tuesday rejected U.S. support for a Canadian drive to ban landmines, saying it feared a "ploy" designed to avert a total ban.

"The new U.S. position on landmines is not acceptable. Handicap International fears that it is only a ploy to sabotage the Ottawa process and thus a complete ban on anti-personnel mines," Handicap International (HI) said in a statement.
The White House said on Monday the United States will participate in the Ottawa process negotiations after staying away from the Canadian initiative for months.
The talks are preparing for the signature of a complete ban on anti-personnel land mines in the Canadian capital in December.
HI, which provides artificial limbs for landmine victims worldwide, said U.S. conditions would weaken the treaty.
"We prefer a strong treaty without the U.S. to a weak treaty with the U.S.," HI spokesman Koen Van den Broeck told Reuters.

U.S. officials said on Monday Washington would insist on an exception for the Korean peninsula, where it has 37,000 troops in South Korea facing the threat of a possible invasion from communist North Korea.
The U.S. also wants to delay a ban on "smart" land mines, which self-destruct after a set time period, until it has developed alternative weapons.

HI said the introduction of a differentiation between classical "dumb" mines and smart mines would considerably weaken the treaty, as a 1980 U.N. Conventional Weapons Convention already forbids the use of dumb mines.
"There is no need to demonstrate that the so-called smart mines make no distinction between the foot of a soldier and the foot of a child," the HI statement said.

HI also said it did not accept a U.S. proposal that the treaty would not take force of law until China and Russia had signed it. "This will slow down, and even completely paralyse, the process," the statement said.
China and Russia are not taking part in the Ottawa process.
The Canadian initiative promises a treaty by the end of the year banning the use, export, production and stockpiling of anti-personnel land mines. It does not cover anti-vehicle mines.

U.S. President Bill Clinton had rejected the Canadian initiative in January, saying it left little room for exceptions sought by U.S. military commanders. Instead, he had used the U.N. Conference on Disarmament in Geneva as the focus of U.S. policy.
A White House official said on Monday the U.S. had concluded there was not enough progress in Geneva in the last six months.
He added Washington was not abandoning the Geneva talks, but would continue on both tracks simultaneously.

The more than 100 countries engaged in the Ottawa process will meet in Oslo on September 1 to discuss the treaty. At that meeting, Washington will argue strongly for an exception for Korea, a U.S. official said.
